exchanges.question: What drove the improvement in the current accident year loss ratio versus 2Q 2025 (lower non-cat property losses, mix, loss picks)? Separately, will the reinsurance ceding commission rate keep rising after the renewals?
exchanges.answer: Allibhai: losses came in below expectations, as for the last few quarters; nothing out of the ordinary, just normal variability and mix across a dozen statutory lines; reserves are as conservative as they've ever been. Petrucelli: Q2 is a good indication going forward; a slight uptick in commissions is possible; treaties renewed June 1st so only one month of new-treaty effect; AI could bring operating efficiency gains; Q2 expense ratio should be a good measure going forward.

exchanges.question: With E&S casualty softening (GWP up 3% vs up 4% in Q1), how much are ROEs compressing, assuming loss trends of high single to low double digits are unchanged? How is Kinsale thinking about broker commissions, given brokers typically seek higher commissions in a soft market and may place more business admitted?
exchanges.answer: Kehoe: Kinsale manages everything to a 20% ROE or greater and most product lines probably run ahead of that; Q2 operating ROE was 24.4%; there is give and take between profit and growth. On commissions he did not give a plan, calling the wholesaler-retailer commission split a normal tension in a soft market, and cited best-in-industry service, quote ratio and response time, the broadest appetite, and growth ex Commercial Property Division.

exchanges.question: Is 2Q the trough in Commercial Property, with pricing less negative in 2027 or a return to larger shared placements? What is driving the 3.7% growth ex Commercial Property, and is business returning to the admitted market?
exchanges.answer: Winston: no telling where it goes in 2027; pressure continues from London MGAs and traditional markets putting up larger limits on shared and layered deals; Kinsale will keep pricing tactical, meet return thresholds and accept shrinking in that division. Long-tail competition from London is creeping into other liability occurrence lines, depressing Construction pricing, with more competition in general casualty; pockets of opportunity remain. Some flow to the admitted market, but not pervasive.

exchanges.question: How much of the increase in inbound accounts comes from broker engagement versus more competitive pricing? What is the view on social inflation and casualty loss trends, and was the better accident year loss ratio entirely short-tail property?
exchanges.answer: Winston: a bit of both; the idle broker initiative is re-engaging brokers, hit ratios are roughly the same for renewal and new business, and more submissions mean more binds. Allibhai: casualty loss cost trend probably mid-single digits, varying by line; less exposed to social inflation given smaller accounts and lower limits; short-tail lines performing especially well across the board. Kehoe: slowing the release of IBNR in longer-tail occurrence business for a couple of years while letting it flow out faster in short-tail lines; the Commercial Property crisis is over and rates are falling dramatically.

exchanges.question: What granularity on property pricing in Q2 versus Q1, and when might it stabilize? Could the current accident year loss ratio drift up given mix shift from property to casualty? How will buyback pacing look if top-line growth stays moderate?
exchanges.answer: Kehoe: equilibrium will eventually come but he has no insight into when; confident in pricing discipline and concentration risk management. Winston: Agribusiness Property and small business property are more stable; Inland Marine is seeing a little more competition across five product buckets; people are starting to get to the floor of property pricing but London pressure persists. Allibhai: the loss ratio could drift up over time, but losses are below expectations. Kehoe on buyback: will keep leaning in; first $100 million authorization exhausted, then $250 million with about $80 million left, plus the new $250 million; growth would be the first priority when it accelerates; small dividend also paid.

exchanges.question: How have new products contributed to growth over the past year, and what is the potential growth uplift going forward?
exchanges.answer: Winston: Kinsale does not jump in feet first; the pace is crawl, walk, run. New products are driving submissions and new premium, but growth will be slow, and Kinsale will ramp up as the market turns. No quantification of past contribution or future uplift was given.
